Instead, I will press on the fault line you have exposed but not fully examined: the distinction between a manageable legitimacy deficit and a fatal one, and the claim that constitutional language can subordinate national character to individual equality without the former ceasing to be constitutive.

**1. The hierarchy you propose is logically unstable.**

You argue that the particularist self-definition must not function as a justiciable counterweight in rights adjudication—that Jewish national character must be expressly subordinated to individual equality in cases of conflict. But you simultaneously maintain that the state’s *raison d’être* is Jewish self-determination. These two commitments cannot coexist in the way you describe.

If the state’s foundational purpose is the self-determination of the Jewish nation, then that purpose must, at some point, have operative legal force. A constitutional principle that is always subordinated to another principle in every case of conflict is not a constitutional principle at all—it is decorative text. You cannot claim the state exists *for* Jewish self-determination while simultaneously insisting that this purpose must yield *whenever* it encounters an individual equality claim. Either the purpose has weight, in which case it will sometimes prevail and thus function as a justiciable counterweight, or it has no weight, in which case the state’s declared *raison d’être* is a fiction.

The "strict and fragile conditions" you specify are not conditions at all—they are a description of a state that has ceased to be a nation-state in any meaningful constitutional sense and has become a liberal state with vestigial national symbolism. That may be a defensible model, but it is not the model you set out to defend. You have not shown that the nation-state model is compatible with democratic legitimacy; you have shown that a state that *calls* itself a nation-state while functionally operating as a liberal state can be legitimate. That is a different claim entirely.

**2. The "constitutive we" cannot be acknowledged as exclusionary and simultaneously rendered harmless.**

You concede that the Arab citizen is constitutionally excluded from the sovereign "we" and that this imposes a genuine democratic deficit. Your proposed remedy is that this deficit be "transparently acknowledged" and "institutionally compensated" through robust equality enforcement. But you have not explained how acknowledgement and compensation address the structural problem.

The structural problem is not that the Arab citizen *feels* excluded. It is that she *is* excluded from the sovereign subject in whose name the state acts. When the state makes decisions—about immigration, about land allocation, about the boundaries of the political community, about what counts as a national priority—it does so in the name of a "we" that constitutionally does not include her. No quantum of individual rights enforcement can alter this fact. An individual right to non-discrimination in employment or housing does not give her co-ownership of the sovereign subject. It gives her protection against some of the consequences of her exclusion, which is precisely what makes her status structurally secondary: she is a rights-bearing object of governance, not a co-author of sovereignty.

Your model offers the Arab citizen the most generous possible terms of second-class citizenship—and then asks us to call that democratic legitimacy. The term is not accurate. What you are describing is a liberal autocracy for the excluded minority: benevolent, rights-respecting, procedurally fair, but autocratic nonetheless, because the minority is governed by a sovereign "we" it cannot join without ceasing to be itself.

**3. The scalar approach to legitimacy masks a categorical boundary.**

You propose that democratic legitimacy is scalar, not binary, and that the deficit created by national exclusion can be compensated but not eliminated. This framing allows you to avoid the question of where the threshold of categorical illegitimacy lies, and to treat the Nation-State Law as a matter of degree rather than kind.

But some deficits are not compensable by degrees because they are definitional. The question is not *how much* exclusion from the sovereign "we" is compatible with democratic legitimacy. The question is whether a political order that constitutionally assigns sovereignty to one ethnically-defined nation can be a democracy for those outside that nation *at all*. Your scalar framework presupposes that this is a quantitative question about how much exclusion, how much compensation, how much contestation. But it is a qualitative question about the nature of the political relationship.

If the state's sovereignty is vested in the Jewish nation—not the citizenry as a whole—then non-Jewish citizens are not participants in sovereignty. They are participants in governance under a sovereignty that is not theirs. That is not a deficit within democracy; that is a departure from the democratic principle that sovereignty resides in the people as a whole. You can call that departure manageable or unmanageable, compensable or incompensable. But you cannot call the resulting arrangement a democracy for the excluded, because the defining feature of democracy—popular sovereignty—does not include them.

**4. Your reform proposal inadvertently proves my point.**

You propose that the deficit be remedied by "explicit constitutional language subordinating Jewish national character to individual equality in cases of conflict." Notice what this does: it elevates individual equality—a universal citizenship principle—above Jewish national character—the particularist principle. In cases of conflict, the universal principle wins.

But if the universal principle always wins in cases of conflict, then it is the universal principle that is constitutionally sovereign, and the particularist principle is constitutionally subordinate. That is not a nation-state with robust individual rights. That is a liberal state with a national flavor. The Jewish character becomes ornamental—something the state *professes* but cannot *enforce* when it matters. And if the Jewish character can never be enforced when it matters, then in what sense is the state a nation-state?

You have not defended the nation-state model. You have proposed that a nation-state can be legitimate only if it ceases to function as a nation-state in any legally operative sense—that is, only if its national character is reduced to symbolism that always yields to universal citizenship principles. That is an argument for liberal universalism wearing a kippah, not for the democratic legitimacy of the nation-state.

**5. The fragility of your conditions is itself evidence of structural incompatibility.**

You describe the conditions under which the nation-state model might be legitimate as "strict and fragile." But fragility is precisely what my argument predicts. If the structure creates a permanent incentive for the majority to operationalize its national character at the minority's expense, then the conditions you specify will always be under threat. The Nation-State Law is not an aberration; it is the predictable expression of the logic you claim can be contained.

A model that is only legitimate under conditions that the model itself systematically undermines is not a legitimate model. It is a model in permanent contradiction with itself. The fact that Israel "currently fails to fully meet" your conditions is not a contingent failure of implementation. It is the working-out of a structural logic that your conditions attempt to suppress but cannot eliminate, because the logic arises from the very constitutional self-definition you seek to preserve.

**The core of my position, after all these exchanges, is this:**

You have moved from defending the nation-state model to defending a model in which national character is constitutionally subordinate to universal equality in every operative context—which is to say, a model that is no longer a nation-state in any sense that distinguishes it from a liberal state with majority-group cultural dominance. Your argument succeeds only by evacuating the nation-state of its defining feature: the capacity of the national "we" to act as a sovereign subject in its own name. What remains is a liberal state whose majority happens to be Jewish and whose constitutional text retains vestigial national language that must yield whenever it is invoked. That may be a defensible vision of Israel. It is not a defense of the nation-state principle you set out to vindicate.

The legitimacy deficit you acknowledge is not compensable because it is not a deficit in the quantitative sense your scalar framework requires. It is the categorical absence of the relationship—shared sovereignty—that constitutes democratic citizenship in the first place. No amount of individual rights can substitute for membership in the sovereign people, because individual rights protect the individual against the sovereign; they do not make the individual part of the sovereign. You are offering a sophisticated defense of enlightened guardianship, not democratic legitimacy.

The constraint on the second arena does not empty the first of meaning. The Law of Return is not a courtroom counterweight; it is a statutory expression of national purpose that operates independently of rights adjudication. The flag is not a justiciable principle; it is a symbol that shapes public culture without entering judicial balancing.

The Nation-State Law's error, on this account, is not that it affirms Jewish national character. It is that it introduces that character into the constitutional text at a level that invites its use as a justiciable principle in the one arena where it does not belong: the adjudication of individual claims. The problem is jurisdictional, not substantive. The remedy is not to strip Jewish character of all operative force; it is to confine its operative force to the arenas where it legitimately operates and to constitutionally wall it off from rights adjudication.

This requires a clearer statement than I have given of what "subordinating Jewish national character to individual equality in cases of conflict" means. That does not mean Jewish national character has no constitutional weight anywhere. It means it has no weight as a defense against an individual rights claim. Its weight operates in the legislative arena, where immigration law is written; in the administrative arena, where land is allocated; in the cultural arena, where symbols are chosen. What they are not part of is the ethnos, the national community in whose name the state narrates its founding purpose. Let us examine the empirical foundation you claim cannot be adjudicated. You treat the heterogeneity of Arab political leadership as evidence that the threat perception is overstated. That is precisely the vulnerability. Heterogeneity does not neutralize threat; it masks it. When a minority population contains factions that participate in coalition governance alongside factions that openly align with the state's declared enemies, the liberal inclusion strategy does not co-opt the hostile—it provides them with institutional platforms, legal protections, and political legitimacy from which to advance their project incrementally. The communist and liberal factions demanding a "state of all its citizens" do not merely request equality; they demand the constitutional liquidation of Jewish national self-determination as the state's organizing principle. The distinction you insist upon—between contesting ethnic character and seeking destruction—collapses when the state's ethnic character is its reason for existing. The critique's strongest point is about reversibility. You object to my collapsing the distinction between absolute monarchy and constitutional democracy as “merely” technologies of rule, insisting that these differences are analytically fundamental. This is the heart of your confusion. The distinction between technologies of rule is indeed analytically useful—for comparing different structures of domination. A feudal serf bound to the land is in a different legal reality than a wage laborer in a capitalist democracy. But to observe that the wage laborer is not a serf is not to prove the wage laborer is free. It is to prove that systems of domination evolve more sophisticated, less legible technologies. When I say that Arab citizens’ rights and agency are management techniques, I am not saying they are trivial in lived experience. I am saying they are functional within a system whose foundational objective—the preservation of Jewish national supremacy—remains unrevisable by those subjected to it. The fact that you cannot democratically dissolve the state’s Jewish character is not merely a “ceiling”; it is the constitutional equivalent of a one-way mirror. The majority can see through it and act; the minority can only see their own reflection. Your claim that this is “the ordinary condition of democratic politics” is a definitional fiat that empties democracy of its normative content. You are describing a system in which the subordinated group can, through extraordinary effort and political coalition-building, secure modest improvements in the terms of their subordination. A structure that permanently assigns one group to the status of national authors and another to the status of tolerated participants, and that immunizes that assignment from democratic dissolution, is not a defective democracy. It is a constitutional ethnocracy. To call it anything less is to abandon the analytical vocabulary of political science for the apologetics of managed inequality. The ceiling is not a detail. It is the definition of the room.
